<p class="eyebrow">CAUSAL SHAP · A SPACEFLIGHT RISK BENCHMARK</p>

# What can a prediction ranking tell us about changing risk?

<p class="lede">We compare explanations of a model's predictions with the effects of changing variables in a causal model. NASA's renal-stone graph provides the structure for simulations in which those effects are known.</p>

<p class="hero-route">The central workflow connects the teaching example below to the study's completed comparisons, open questions and classroom materials.</p>
<nav class="reading-route" aria-label="On this page"><a href="#path">Central workflow</a><a href="#worked-example">Worked example</a><a href="#depth">Path length</a><a href="#evidence">Simulation results</a><a href="#claims">Remaining work</a><a href="#educators">Educator guide</a><a href="#resources">Code and records</a></nav>
:::

::: {.panel .goals-panel #goals}
<p class="eyebrow">THE QUESTION</p>

## A cause can receive little predictive credit.

<p class="deck">In this four-node teaching chain, X affects Y through A and M. If M is measured exactly and carries the entire effect, a predictor can rely on M while an intervention on X can still change Y.</p>

```{=html}
<figure class="chain-figure">
  <object id="chain-animation" data="assets/two-goals.svg" type="image/svg+xml" width="760" height="300" aria-label="Four-node chain comparing predictive and structural credit">
    <p>X → A → M → Y. A predictor can use M alone. Setting X can still change Y through A and M.</p>
  </object>
  <div class="chain-controls" hidden>
    <button type="button" id="chain-play">Play comparison</button>
    <button type="button" data-chain-view="prediction">Show prediction</button>
    <button type="button" data-chain-view="intervention">Show structural credit</button>
    <span id="chain-status" role="status">Prediction view</span>
  </div>
  <figcaption><strong>Schematic illustration.</strong> Bar heights are not measured SHAP values or effect sizes, and totals are not comparable across phases. The orange phase illustrates possible structural credit, not an action recommendation.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div class="goal-grid">
  <section class="goal"><h3>Explaining a prediction</h3><p>An ideal predictor using M alone does not use X or A. Model-interventional SHAP gives unused inputs zero credit. Conditional SHAP can give them credit through their associations.</p></section>
  <section class="goal intervention"><h3>Estimating a change</h3><p>Setting X changes the downstream variables according to the assumed equations. The resulting change in Y is an intervention effect. Structural attribution distributes credit using a specified causal game; that credit is not the effect of an action.</p></section>
</div>
```

<details class="math-note">
<summary>Assumptions behind the chain</summary>

For $A=aX+\varepsilon_A$, $M=bA+\varepsilon_M$, and $Y=cM+\varepsilon_Y$, with mutually independent mean-zero disturbances and X independent of them, $Y\perp(X,A)\mid M$. The slope of the mean response to setting X is $abc$. This is full mediation in an affine chain; noisy measurement, additional paths, nonlinear responses and fitted-model behavior can change the conclusion. The renal comparisons below include credit shifts in both directions. [Derivation and scope](https://github.com/ahhatype/causal-shap-spaceflight-renal-stones/blob/main/docs/playbook/central-workflow.md).

</details>
:::

::: {.panel #path}
<p class="eyebrow">THE CENTRAL WORKFLOW</p>

## From a prediction explanation to an evaluated intervention

<p class="deck">These seven stages organize the project. The simulations assess parts of this workflow; they do not yet validate it end to end. A supplied graph can be tested directly, and discovery and expert review may require several iterations.</p>

```{=html}
<ol class="central-workflow">
  <li><span class="stage-number">01</span><div><h3>Define the study</h3><p>Specify the outcome, graph assumptions and changes to compare. The renal example uses cumulative mission days and nephrolithiasis.</p></div><span class="stage-status">Completed</span></li>
  <li><span class="stage-number">02</span><div><h3>Fit and explain predictions</h3><p>Compare what different fitted models credit. Five model–explainer pairings have run on the 14-node working subgraph.</p></div><span class="stage-status">Completed</span></li>
  <li><span class="stage-number">03</span><div><h3>Examine candidate graphs</h3><p>Assess structures under stated discovery assumptions. The Step 6 diagnostic disconnected the binary outcome; the broader Step 8 working-subgraph comparison remains pending.</p></div><span class="stage-status">Partial</span></li>
  <li><span class="stage-number">04</span><div><h3>Reconsider excluded candidates</h3><p>A proposed detector and two-channel filter would flag candidates for further review. Neither has evaluated results.</p></div><span class="stage-status placeholder">Placeholder</span></li>
  <li><span class="stage-number">05</span><div><h3>Review graph assumptions</h3><p>Record biological evidence and unresolved directions. Round 1 uses unrevised causal inputs; rounds two and three use a scripted heuristic. No human reviewed these rounds.</p></div><span class="stage-status">Partial</span></li>
  <li><span class="stage-number">06</span><div><h3>Follow changes through the graph</h3><p>Distinguish ordering-based attribution from propagation through structural equations. The full-DAG propagation result is a prototype.</p></div><span class="stage-status">Partial</span></li>
  <li><span class="stage-number">07</span><div><h3>Evaluate feasible actions</h3><p>Estimate a specified action's benefit, uncertainty and cost. Attribution can inform this step but cannot replace it.</p></div><span class="stage-status placeholder">Future work</span></li>
</ol>
```

Robustness checks apply across the stages. Nonlinear-generator comparisons and broader data-constraint sweeps remain pending. A prediction study can finish after stage 2; causal analysis need not begin with SHAP. The [workflow and evidence map](https://github.com/ahhatype/causal-shap-spaceflight-renal-stones/blob/main/docs/playbook/central-workflow.md) links each stage to the examples. The [protocol crosswalk](https://github.com/ahhatype/causal-shap-spaceflight-renal-stones/blob/main/docs/playbook/README.md#the-seven-steps-one-flow-five-tellings) maps this presentation to the original 13-step plan and the six-rung framework.
:::

::: {.panel #worked-example}
<p class="eyebrow">A WORKED EXAMPLE</p>

## A two-player calculation

The classroom example combines A into the X-to-M relationship, leaving $X\to M\to Y$. Let $M=0.6X+\varepsilon_M$ and $Y=0.6M+\varepsilon_Y$, with independent mean-zero disturbances. For a synthetic observation with $x=1$ and $\varepsilon_M=0.2$, we observe $m=0.8$ and the ideal predictor $f=0.6M$ gives 0.48.

| Calculation | X | M | What it answers |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Model-interventional Shapley credit | 0 | 0.48 | Which inputs contribute to this prediction? |
| Symmetric structural Shapley credit | 0.18 | 0.30 | How does a specified causal game distribute credit? |
| Mean effect of setting X from 0 to 1 | 0.36 | — | How much does the expected outcome change? |

The Shapley rows each sum to the same prediction relative to a zero background. The intervention contrast is a separate quantity. When both X and M are set in the structural game, M stays at its set value; it is not updated again from X. The [worksheet and answer key](https://github.com/ahhatype/causal-shap-spaceflight-renal-stones/tree/main/docs/classroom) show every coalition value.

This example makes stages 1, 2 and 6 calculable by hand, using an ideal predictor in place of fitting one in stage 2. It uses a known graph and does not run discovery, expert review, the detector or action selection. Its symmetric game is not a numerical reproduction of the full-DAG prototype. The next sections show what changes when we add longer paths, competing predictors and a spaceflight risk graph.
:::

::: {.panel #depth}
<p class="eyebrow">PATH LENGTH AND SAMPLE SIZE</p>

## Path length and detection

<p class="deck">This is a power problem distinct from predictive screening-off: the upstream effect really is smaller in this example. Each added link multiplies the effect by 0.6, so more data are needed to distinguish it from sampling noise.</p>

```{=html}
<div class="depth-grid">
  <figure class="depth-effects">
    <h3>More links, smaller effects</h3>
    <p class="figure-subtitle">Standardized chain · 0.6 per edge</p>
    <svg class="depth-chain-sketch" id="depth-chain-sketch" viewBox="0 0 450 76" role="img" aria-labelledby="depth-sketch-title">
      <title id="depth-sketch-title">Each added upstream link multiplies the total effect by 0.6. The outcome stays at the right.</title>
      <g class="depth-link" data-depth="5"><path d="M37 34Q58 32 80 34 M74 30L80 34L74 38"/><circle cx="20" cy="34" r="15"/><text x="20" y="40">5</text></g>
      <g class="depth-link" data-depth="4"><path d="M116 34Q138 32 161 34 M155 30L161 34L155 38"/><circle cx="99" cy="34" r="15"/><text x="99" y="40">4</text></g>
      <g class="depth-link" data-depth="3"><path d="M197 34Q220 32 242 34 M236 30L242 34L236 38"/><circle cx="180" cy="34" r="15"/><text x="180" y="40">3</text></g>
      <g class="depth-link" data-depth="2"><path d="M278 34Q300 32 323 34 M317 30L323 34L317 38"/><circle cx="261" cy="34" r="15"/><text x="261" y="40">2</text></g>
      <g class="depth-link" data-depth="1"><path d="M359 34Q381 32 403 34 M397 30L403 34L397 38"/><circle cx="342" cy="34" r="15"/><text x="342" y="40">1</text></g>
      <circle class="sketch-outcome" cx="422" cy="34" r="16"/><text class="sketch-outcome-label" x="422" y="40">Y</text>
      <text x="12" y="70" class="sketch-direction">farther upstream</text><text x="437" y="70" class="sketch-direction" text-anchor="end">outcome</text>
    </svg>
    <ol class="effect-bars" aria-label="Total effect by directed distance to the outcome">
      <li><span class="effect-value">0.60</span><span class="effect-track" aria-hidden="true"><span style="height:100%"></span></span><span>1 hop</span></li>
      <li><span class="effect-value">0.36</span><span class="effect-track" aria-hidden="true"><span style="height:60%"></span></span><span>2 hops</span></li>
      <li><span class="effect-value">0.22</span><span class="effect-track" aria-hidden="true"><span style="height:36%"></span></span><span>3 hops</span></li>
      <li><span class="effect-value">0.13</span><span class="effect-track" aria-hidden="true"><span style="height:21.6%"></span></span><span>4 hops</span></li>
      <li><span class="effect-value">0.08</span><span class="effect-track" aria-hidden="true"><span style="height:12.96%"></span></span><span>5 hops</span></li>
    </ol>
    <button class="motion-control" type="button" data-motion="depth" aria-controls="depth-chain-sketch" hidden>Replay: one more link</button>
    <figcaption>Total effect = 0.6<sup>depth</sup>. Across a general graph, different paths can add or cancel.</figcaption>
  </figure>
  <figure class="depth-detection">
    <h3>Smaller effects need more data</h3>
    <p class="figure-subtitle">Teaching simulation · selected depths</p>
    <img src="assets/depth-detection.svg" width="500" height="310" loading="lazy" alt="Detection rises with sample size. At 25 observations, depths 1, 3 and 5 are detected in approximately 93%, 19% and 8% of replicates; all reach 100% at 4,000 in this teaching simulation.">
    <figcaption>Detection by a marginal-slope test, over 400 replicates per sample size. This measures sampling uncertainty, not causal-discovery accuracy.</figcaption>
  </figure>
</div>
```

<p>A small or undetected marginal effect at one sample size is not enough reason to exclude a candidate cause.</p>

<p class="section-note">The example uses linear mechanisms; it does not say the best action is always upstream. Measurement error adds estimation difficulty. <a href="assets/depth_washout.svg">View all five depths and the original simulation details</a>.</p>
:::

<p class="eyebrow">THE RENAL SIMULATIONS AND A SEPARATE STRESS TEST</p>

## What the simulations show.

<p class="deck">NASA supplies the renal-stone topology. We choose the simulation coefficients, giving each testbed a known total-effect answer key. These are simulation results, not measured astronaut effects.</p>

```{=html}
<p class="section-note">The working subgraph is scoped and augmented, with separately specified coefficients; it is not an unchanged subset of the full simulator. The full-DAG clean-v3 data have 10,000 records (generation seed 20260710). The <a href="https://github.com/ahhatype/causal-shap-spaceflight-renal-stones/blob/main/docs/playbook/central-workflow.md#what-information-each-comparison-receives">comparison-inputs record</a> states what graph and mechanism information each method receives.</p>
<div class="evidence-groups">
  <section class="evidence-group">
    <div class="testbed-heading"><h3>Working subgraph</h3><span>14 nodes · diagnostics</span></div>
    <div class="finding"><p class="finding-number">Model dependent<small>direction of misplaced credit</small></p><div><h4>The ranking follows the fitted model.</h4><p>One chain gives a parent almost no credit; on another, four of five model–explainer pairings shift credit toward the parent. One seed.</p></div></div>
    <div class="finding"><p class="finding-number">0 edges<small>adjacent to the outcome</small></p><div><h4>A discovery configuration disconnects Y.</h4><p>At n = 1,000 (seed 20260812), Gaussian PC leaves the binary outcome isolated. Ng et al.'s Causal SHAP then returns all zeros. This diagnoses one test configuration, including its suitability for a binary outcome.</p></div></div>
    <div class="finding"><p class="finding-number">Mixed changes<small>scripted revisions · XGBoost</small></p><div><h4>Revising causal inputs does not always help.</h4><p>From round 1 to round 3, Kendall’s τ changes from 0.231 to 0.205 for ASV, from 0.077 to 0.154 for Shapley Flow, and from undefined to 0.714 for Ng et al. Rounds two and three use a scripted heuristic standing in for expert review, consulting the known graph or errors against truth. Method budgets and revision rules differ. No human reviewed these rounds.</p></div></div>
  </section>
  <section class="evidence-group">
    <div class="testbed-heading"><h3>Source DAG</h3><span>51 nodes · NASA-topology simulation</span></div>
    <div class="finding"><p class="finding-number">0.506 / 0.528<small>Kendall's τ · ordinary / ordering-only</small></p><div><h4>No detected difference in the matched comparison.</h4><p>Both explain the same fitted XGBoost model, with 64 evaluation records, 128 background records and 128 permutations each. The ordering variant receives the true graph’s constraints. The paired-bootstrap interval includes zero.</p></div></div>
    <div class="finding prototype-finding"><p class="finding-number">τ 0.794<small>structural propagation prototype</small></p><div><h4>Propagation with known mechanisms.</h4><p>Top-five recovery is 1.00. This prototype uses 32 evaluation records, 32 background records and 32 permutations. It propagates interventions using the supplied graph and known simulation mechanisms, then scores the fitted XGBoost model. Its additional information and smaller budget prevent interpreting its score as method superiority over the ordering comparison. It does not recover unknown mechanisms and has no repeated-seed uncertainty.</p></div></div>
  </section>
  <section class="evidence-group">
    <div class="testbed-heading"><h3>Teaching case</h3><span>5-node stress test</span></div>
    <div class="finding"><p class="finding-number">45.6%<small>of ordinary SHAP mass</small></p><div><h4>Prediction can credit a non-cause.</h4><p>A node caused by the outcome receives this credit despite having zero total effect. A deliberately pedagogic example.</p></div></div>
  </section>
</div>
```

<p class="section-note">Both renal outcomes are binary. The ranking target is the absolute difference in simulated nephrolithiasis probability between specified high and low settings, using 50,000 common-random-number draws. The working subgraph uses ±1 SD for continuous variables; the full DAG uses Q25 versus Q75. Binary contrasts use 0 versus 1. These contrasts and SHAP output scales are not interchangeable.</p>

<p class="section-note">Kendall's τ measures rank agreement with the frozen total-effect truth within each testbed. <a href="https://github.com/ahhatype/causal-shap-spaceflight-renal-stones/blob/main/docs/full_dag/RESEARCH_RECORD.md">Full-DAG results</a> · <a href="https://github.com/ahhatype/causal-shap-spaceflight-renal-stones/blob/main/docs/step04_results.md">Working-subgraph attribution</a> · <a href="https://github.com/ahhatype/causal-shap-spaceflight-renal-stones/blob/main/docs/step06_results.md">Scripted expert-loop results</a>.</p>
:::

::: {.panel #educators}
<p class="eyebrow">EDUCATOR GUIDE</p>

## A 50-minute classroom lesson

The starter kit includes an offline interactive lab, a student worksheet, an educator guide with answers, and a Python script using only the standard library. Learners should know regression, conditional expectation and basic causal graphs. No astronaut data, proprietary tool or SHAP installation is required.

| Time | Activity |
| --- | --- |
| 0–5 min | Ask whether X should receive predictive credit before revealing the calculation. |
| 5–15 min | Work through the predictive coalition values in the worksheet. |
| 15–25 min | Compare structural credit with the intervention contrast; explain why 0.18 and 0.36 differ. |
| 25–35 min | Try zero and negative coefficients, then a direct nonlinear response. |
| 35–45 min | Examine two observationally identical Gaussian models with different causal directions; inspect the research status below. |
| 45–50 min | Ask learners to state one assumption and propose a test of a provisional research result. |

For a 90-minute lab, add 20 minutes modifying the Python examples and 20 minutes tracing one renal result to its source. The four-node animation, the two-player worksheet and the five-node stress test have different roles; none is the renal simulation.

<p class="resource-links"><a href="resources/causal-shap-classroom.zip" download>Download the complete classroom kit</a> · <a href="https://github.com/ahhatype/causal-shap-spaceflight-renal-stones/blob/main/docs/classroom/educator-guide.md">Educator guide and answer key</a> · <a href="https://github.com/ahhatype/causal-shap-spaceflight-renal-stones/blob/main/docs/classroom/worksheet.md">Student worksheet</a></p>

Unzip the kit and open `index.html` for the interactive lesson. Run `python lab.py --check` for the text-only analytic checks. This is a lesson prototype; coauthor-reviewed slides and a guided renal-reproduction notebook remain to be developed.

<details class="math-note"><summary>Three discussion prompts</summary>

- **Does a direct arrow imply a straight response?** No. A direct structural relationship can be curved; the graph and the response function specify different assumptions.
- **Does a longer pathway always have a smaller effect?** No. Attenuation in the chain requires coefficients below one in magnitude; paths can also reinforce or cancel.
- **Does a better prediction imply a better intervention estimate?** No. Evaluate both against the appropriate target; the nonlinear robustness analysis is still pending.

</details>
:::
